nodes.name: 20210218195106-capture-up.sql
nodes.summary: Creates the core capture table storing tree-capture observations with GPS location, imagery, planter and species metadata, plus seven supporting indexes.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses a GiST index on estimated_geometric_location for PostGIS geospatial queries.

nodes.summary: Rollback migration that drops the capture table and its indexes.

nodes.name: 20210219042951-domain-event-down.sql
nodes.summary: Rollback migration that drops the domain_event table and related partitions.

nodes.name: 20210219043110-tree-up.sql

nodes.summary: Rollback migration that drops the tree table and its indexes.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README to learn what the TreeTracker API does and how it is built. It presents a Node.js/Express microservice over PostgreSQL, describes the layered MVC-like architecture, and documents the setup, migration, and seeding workflows. Use it as the roadmap for the rest of this tour.

tour.title: Bootstrap and Express Wiring
tour.description: server.js is the runtime entry point. It loads environment config, initializes logging, and starts the Express app on the configured port. app.js is the application factory that wires the middleware chain: content-type validation, Swagger UI, JSON body parsing, the main router, the error handler, and the domain event handlers registered on startup. Together they show how a request enters the system.

tour.title: Routing and API Surface
tour.description: Building on app.js, the routing layer maps URLs to handlers. routes/index.js is a barrel that aggregates every feature router into one array for mounting, and treeRoutes.js is a representative router that wires tree and tree-tag URLs to their handlers. swaggerDoc.js assembles the per-handler OpenAPI definitions into the single spec served at the docs endpoint, so the API contract stays close to the routes.

tour.title: Request Handlers and Validation
tour.description: Follow the tree request into its handler. treeHandler/index.js holds the Express handlers for tree CRUD, potential-match lookup, and tree-tag endpoints. schemas.js defines the Joi validation schemas that guard query parameters and request bodies before any business logic runs, and docs.js supplies the Swagger path definitions surfaced in Step 3. This is where HTTP concerns end and the domain begins.
tour.languageLesson: Joi schemas describe expected shapes declaratively. Validating at the handler boundary keeps invalid input out of the service and model layers, so downstream code can trust its arguments.

tour.title: The Service Layer
tour.description: Handlers delegate to services. TreeService.js coordinates tree CRUD, potential-match queries, and queue integration over a single database session, keeping transaction boundaries and cross-cutting orchestration out of the handlers. HttpError.js is the custom error type that services and handlers throw; it carries a status code and a rollback flag that the error middleware from Step 2 uses to unwind transactions.

tour.title: Domain Models and Repositories
tour.description: Beneath the service sit the model and repository layers. models/tree.js holds the domain logic for querying, creating, updating, and matching trees, delegating persistence to TreeRepository.js. That repository extends BaseRepository.js, the generic Knex-backed base class that gives every entity getById, filtered queries, counting, create, and update primitives. This inheritance is the backbone of the data-access layer.
tour.languageLesson: The repository pattern isolates SQL details behind a stable interface. A shared BaseRepository centralizes common query logic, so concrete repositories only add entity-specific queries such as the tree potential-match lookup.

tour.title: Database Connection and Transactions
tour.description: Repositories run their queries through the infra layer. knex.js configures and exports the shared Knex/Postgres connection used across the service. Session.js wraps that connection to manage the transaction lifecycle (begin, commit, rollback) that the service layer in Step 5 relies on, tying the rollback flag from HttpError back to real database behavior.

tour.title: Database Schema and Seed Data
tour.description: The queries above operate on a schema defined by SQL migrations. The tree migration creates the core tree table with a reference to its latest capture, GPS location, species, status, and geospatial indexes; this is the physical shape behind the tree model from Step 6. The seed fixture supplies sample tree records so a fresh database is immediately usable for development and tests.
tour.languageLesson: Migrations evolve the schema in ordered, reversible steps (each has an up and a down file). Seed data is separate from migrations: migrations define structure, seeds populate content for local runs and tests.

tour.title: Asynchronous Messaging
tour.description: Beyond the request cycle, the service communicates through events. QueueService.js owns the RabbitMQ lifecycle and publishes and subscribes to domain events such as capture-created and tree-created, updating DomainEvent status on publish. RabbitMQ.js wraps the rascal Broker with publish, subscribe, and teardown primitives, EventHandlerService.js dispatches queued messages to their handlers, and DomainEvent.js persists the event records.
tour.languageLesson: Persisting a domain event and its status alongside the business write is the outbox idea: the record proves an event should be published, so a failed broker call can be retried without losing the event.

tour.title: Image Upload to S3
tour.description: Grower and capture images live in object storage rather than the database. s3.js instantiates the shared AWS S3 client from environment credentials, and S3Service.js exposes a thin uploadImage helper over it. GrowerAccountImageService.js shows the pattern in action: it uploads the file to S3 and persists the record inside one transaction, rolling back and cleaning up the temp file if either step fails.

tour.title: Testing Approach
tour.description: The project is verified with end-to-end integration tests. tree.spec.js seeds trees, captures, tags, and domain events, then exercises the tree endpoints to assert real API behavior across every layer covered so far. __tests__/utils.js is the shared helper that inserts and deletes trees and captures over Knex and converts POINT strings into PostGIS geometry for the geospatial columns from Step 8.

tour.title: Containerization, CI, and Deployment
tour.description: Finally, see how the service ships. The Dockerfile builds the API on node:16-alpine and runs it with 'node .'. The pull-request CI workflow installs dependencies and runs ESLint, migrations, and the test suite against Postgres and RabbitMQ service containers. The Kubernetes deployment runs two replicas wired to database and RabbitMQ sealed secrets, and the kustomization base aggregates the deployment, service, RBAC, migration job, and secret manifests into one deployable set.
tour.languageLesson: Kustomize composes Kubernetes manifests from a shared base plus per-environment overlays, avoiding copy-pasted YAML. Running migrations as a separate Job keeps schema changes decoupled from the long-running app pods.
